Agujon needlefish (Tylosurus acus) attains a remarkable maximum body length, with the largest recorded individuals reaching 153 cm [Li = 153 cm], placing this species among the most elongate members of the Belonidae. This extreme linear dimension is accompanied by a correspondingly high body mass, as sexually mature adults in prime condition have been documented at an ultimate wet weight of 5800 grams [Wwi = 5800 grams], a value that underscores the substantial somatic investment required to sustain such a piscivorous, pelagic lifestyle. The allometric relationship between length and mass in this species follows a steep power curve typical of gar-like body plans, where increases in length translate disproportionately into mass gains. Preliminary growth-curve analyses based on otolith readings from specimens collected across the eastern Atlantic suggest that individuals approach this asymptotic size relatively late in life, with the most rapid linear extension occurring during the first two to three years following metamorphosis. Comparative data from congeneric needlefishes indicate that Tylosurus acus is among the larger-bodied members of its genus, exceeding the typical maximum lengths reported for Tylosurus crocodilus by a considerable margin.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Tylosurus acus occurs when individuals attain a total length of 47.3 cm [Lp = 47.3 cm], a size threshold at which the body mass is approximately 150.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 150.4 grams]. This length-based puberty benchmark corresponds to a developmental stage well before the ultimate asymptotic size is reached, reflecting an early commitment to reproductive effort that is characteristic of many fast-growing epipelagic teleosts. Field surveys examining gonadal histology in populations from the Mediterranean Sea have confirmed that both males and females exhibit ripe gonads at this size, with vitellogenesis and spermiation actively underway. The relatively modest body mass at puberty, compared to the ultimate wet weight of 5800 grams [Wwi = 5800 grams], indicates that a substantial proportion of post-pubertal growth occurs concurrently with active reproduction, a pattern consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy in which fecundity increases with maternal size. The timing of this maturation event appears to be influenced by local thermal regimes, with individuals in warmer waters reaching the 47.3 cm threshold somewhat earlier in the calendar year than those from cooler, higher-latitude stocks.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], the embryonic development of Tylosurus acus proceeds rapidly, with eclosion occurring just 4 days [ab = 4 days] after fertilisation. This short incubation period is typical of belonid eggs, which are characterised by a thin, transparent chorion and a rapid cleavage rate that minimises the duration of vulnerability to benthic predators. The newly emerged prolarvae are minute, each weighing only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] at birth, a value derived from the spherical egg diameter of approximately 1 mm. Such an extraordinarily low birth mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the yolk-sac larva, which relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days of exogenous feeding onset. The rapid eclosion and minimal initial mass together suggest a high-risk, high-gain early life history: larvae enter the planktonic environment at a very small size but benefit from an extended pelagic larval duration that potentially facilitates widespread dispersal by ocean currents. Temperature appears to be a critical modulator of this early ontogeny, as deviations from 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C] have been observed to delay hatching by up to 24 hours under experimental conditions.

Reproductive output in Tylosurus acus has been quantified through direct observation of spawning events in captivity at 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], revealing that females produce approximately 33.7 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 33.7 eggs per day] over the course of the spawning season. This daily fecundity figure, when contextualised within the species' known spawning frequency of roughly one event per year [F_R_i = roughly one event per year], indicates an extremely high annual reproductive investment. Each egg is small, with a diameter of approximately 1 mm, and the cumulative annual output likely exceeds several thousand eggs per mature female. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, when maintained at a constant 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], is 15 years [am = 15 years], providing a substantial window for repeated reproductive events across the lifespan. This combination of high per-event fecundity and extended iteroparity aligns with the life-history profile of a pelagic predator that experiences low early-life survival but compensates through high fecundity and a prolonged adult phase. The spawning period itself appears protracted, with gravid individuals collected from May through September in the subtropical Atlantic, suggesting that multiple spawning batches may be released within a single season.

The generational length of Tylosurus acus, while modest compared to large scombrids or billfishes, is substantial for a fish of its relatively slender build and small birth mass. The ecological niche of this species as an epipelagic predator demands a life history that balances rapid early growth with sustained reproductive output over many years. Stable isotope analyses of belonid tissues have revealed that Tylosurus acus occupies a high trophic position, feeding predominantly on small schooling fishes such as clupeids and engraulids, which themselves exhibit fast turnover rates and high productivity in subtropical waters. This dietary regime, coupled with the species' efficient swimming morphology and reduced drag profile, likely facilitates the energetic budget required to maintain such a large asymptotic size and the associated fecundity advantages that come with increased maternal length.
